Seinei|en|Emperor Seinei|WD=Q357273|lt=Emperor Seinei}}) ''Shiraka no Take Hirokuni Oshi Waka Yamato Neko no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Kenzō|en|Emperor Kenzō|WD=Q360966|lt=Emperor Kenzō}}) ''Woke no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Ninken|en|Emperor Ninken|WD=Q357266|lt=Emperor Ninken}}) ''Oke no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 16''': ({{ill|Emperor Buretsu|en|Emperor Buretsu|WD=Q334644|lt=Emperor Buretsu}}) ''Ohatsuse no Waka Sasagi no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 17''': ({{ill|Emperor Keitai|en|Emperor Keitai|WD=Q349277|lt=Emperor Keitai}}) ''Ōdo no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 18''': **([[Emperor Ankan]]) ''Hirokuni Oshi Take Kanahi no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Senka|en|Emperor Senka|WD=Q329728|lt=Emperor Senka}}) ''Take Ohirokuni Oshi Tate no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 19''': ({{ill|Emperor Kinmei|en|Emperor Kinmei|WD=Q329792|lt=Emperor Kinmei}}) ''Amekuni Oshiharaki Hironiwa no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 20''': ([[Emperor Bidatsu]]) ''Nunakakura no Futo Tamashiki no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 21''': **({{ill|Emperor Yōmei|en|Emperor Yōmei|WD=Q349281|lt=Emperor Yōmei}}) ''Tachibana no Toyohi no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Sushun|en|Emperor Sushun|WD=Q349238|lt=Emperor Sushun}}) ''Hatsusebe no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 22''': ({{ill|Empress Suiko|en|Empress Suiko|WD=Q298057|lt=Empress Suiko}}) ''Toyomike Kashikiya Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 23''': ({{ill|Emperor Jomei|en|Emperor Jomei|WD=Q329761|lt=Emperor Jomei}}) ''Okinaga Tarashi Hihironuka no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 24''': ({{ill|Empress Kōgyoku|en|Empress Kōgyoku|WD=Q235296|lt=Empress Kōgyoku}}) ''Ame Toyotakara Ikashi Hitarashi no Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 25''': ([[Emperor Kōtoku]]) ''Ame Yorozu Toyohi no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 26''': ([[:en:Empress Saimei|Empress Saimei]]) ''Ame Toyotakara Ikashi Hitarashi no Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 27''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji}}) ''Ame Mikoto Hirakasuwake no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 28''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}}, first chapter) ''Ama no Nunakahara Oki no Mahito no Sumeramikoto, Kami no maki.'' *'''Chapter 29''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}}, second chapter) ''Ama no Nunakahara Oki no Mahito no Sumeramikoto, Shimo no maki.'' *'''Chapter 30''': ({{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}) ''Takamanohara Hirono Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' ==Process of compilation== === Background === The background of the compilation of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is that Emperor Tenmu ordered 12 people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the empire.<ref>''日本の歴史4 天平の時代'' p.39, {{ill|Shueisha|en|Shueisha|WD=Q844822|lt=Shueisha}}, Towao Sakehara</ref>
''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' notes that "{{lang|ja-Hani|先是一品舍人親王奉勅修日本紀。至是功成奏上。紀卅卷系圖一卷}}" in the part of May 720. It means "Up to that time, <!--一品-->Prince Toneri had been compiling ''Nihongi'' on the orders of the emperor; he completed it, submitting 30 volumes of history and one volume of genealogy".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Keizai Zasshisha |editor-link=:ja:経済雑誌社 |title=Shoku Nihongi |script-title=ja:続日本紀 |series=[[Rikkokushi|National History]] |language=ja |volume=2 |date=1897 |publication-place=Tokyo |publisher=Keizai Zasshisha |url={{NDLDC|991092|/1/187|format=url}} |page=362 |via=[[National Diet Library]] |doi=10.11501/991092 |id={{NDLPID|991092}} |author1=経済雑誌社 }}</ref>
===Sources=== The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is a synthesis of older documents, specifically on the records that had been continuously kept in the Yamato court since the sixth century. It also includes documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. Prior to {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, there were ''{{ill|Tennōki|en|Tennōki|WD=Q6141029|lt=Tennōki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kokki|en|Kokki|WD=Q826177|lt=Kokki}}'' compiled by {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}} and [[Soga no Umako]], but as they were stored in Soga's residence, they were burned at the time of the {{ill|Isshi incident|en|Isshi incident|WD=Q1062771|lt=Isshi incident}} in July 645.
The work's contributors refer to various sources which do not exist today. Among those sources, three [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] documents (''Kudara-ki'', etc.) are cited mainly for the purpose of recording diplomatic affairs.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7jDuhnI6r9UC&q=paekche+nihon&pg=PA40 Sakamoto, Tarō. (1991). ''The Six National Histories of Japan: Rikkokushi,'' John S. Brownlee, tr.] pp. 40–41; [https://books.google.com/books?id=x5mwgfPXK1kC&dq=paekche+nihon+shoki&pg=PA170 Inoue Mitsusada. (1999). "The Century of Reform" in ''The Cambridge History of Japan'', Delmer Brown, ed. Vol. I], p.170.</ref> Textual criticism shows that scholars fleeing the destruction of the Baekje to Yamato wrote these histories and the authors of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} heavily relied upon those sources.<ref>Sakamoto, pp. 40–41.</ref> This must be taken into account in relation to statements referring to old historic rivalries between the ancient {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea}}n kingdoms of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|WD=Q28456|lt=Silla}}, {{ill|Goguryeo|en|Goguryeo|WD=Q28370|lt=Goguryeo}}, and [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]].
Some other sources are cited anonymously as ''aru fumi'' ({{lang|ja-Hani|一書}}; "some document"), in order to keep alternative records for specific incidents.
==Exaggeration of reign lengths== Most scholars agree that the purported founding date of Japan (660 BCE) and the earliest emperors of Japan are mythical.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=wrc6rzKkbgcC&dq=Kigensetsu&pg=PA555 Rimmer, Thomas ''et al.'' (2005). ''The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature''], p. 555 n1.</ref>{{failed verification|sate=February 2015|date=February 2015}}<!-- The exact wording of Note 1 is "Empire Founding Day (Kigensetsu), February 11, was established in 1872 as the anniversary of the legendary Emperor Jinmu's accession to the throne in 660 B.C., which is said to have marked the beginning of the Japanese nation. After the Pacific War, it was abolished and then, in 1966, reinstated as Nation Founding Day (Kenkoku kinen no hi)." -- How anyone could read this as supporting the material in this sentence I don't know. --> This does not necessarily imply that the persons referred to did not exist, merely that there is insufficient material available for further verification and study.<ref name="kelly">Kelly, Charles F. [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/kofun.html "Kofun Culture,"] [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/index.htm Japanese Archaeology.] April 27, 2009.</ref> Dates in the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} before the late 7th century were likely recorded using the {{ill|Genka calendar|en|Genka calendar|WD=Q2513041|lt=Genka calendar}} system.<ref>Barnes, Gina Lee. (2007). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GLAo-bLJw4EC&dq=genka+reki&pg=PA226 ''State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite,'' p. 226 n.5].</ref>
For those monarchs, and also for the Emperors {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Ōjin}} and {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Nintoku}}, the lengths of reign are likely to have been exaggerated in order to make the origins of the imperial family sufficiently ancient to satisfy numerological expectations. It is widely believed that the [[:en:Epoch (reference date)|epoch]] of 660 BCE was chosen because it is a "xīn-yǒu" year in the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Sexagenary cycle}}, which according to [[:en:Taoist|Taoist]] beliefs was an appropriate year for a revolution to take place. As Taoist theory also groups together 21 sexagenary cycles into one unit of time, it is assumed that the compilers of {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} assigned the year 601 (a "xīn-yǒu" year in which Prince Shotoku's reformation took place) as a "modern revolution" year, and consequently recorded 660 BCE, 1260 years prior to that year, as the founding epoch.
===''Kesshi Hachidai''=== For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, only the years of birth and reign, year of naming as Crown Prince, names of consorts, and locations of tomb are recorded. They are called the ''Kesshi Hachidai'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|欠史八代}}, "eight generations lacking history") because no legends (or a few, as quoted in ''[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]''{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}) are associated with them. Some{{which|date=February 2015}} studies support the view that these emperors were invented to push Jimmu's reign further back to the year 660 BCE. {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} itself somewhat elevates the "tenth" {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin}}, recording that he was called the ''Hatsu-Kuni-Shirasu'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|御肇国}}: first nation-ruling) emperor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_oEfAAAAYAAJ |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |date=1896 |publisher=Society |isbn=978-0-524-05347-8 |language=en}}</ref>
== Influences == The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Yorke |first=Christopher |title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time |date=February 2006 |url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |access-date=2009-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2006-05-16}}</ref>

[[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Page from a copy of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (c. 9th century)]] {{Shintoism}} The {{nihongo|'''''Nihon Shoki'''''|日本書紀}} or {{Nihongo|'''''Nihongi'''''|日本紀}}, sometimes translated as '''''The Chronicles of Japan''''', is the second-oldest book of classical {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}. It is more elaborate and detailed than the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, the oldest, and has proven to be an important tool for historians and [[:en:Archaeologists|Archaeologists]] as it includes the most complete extant historical record of [[:en:Ancient Japan|Ancient Japan]]. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was finished in [[:en:720 in poetry|720]] under the editorial supervision of {{ill|Prince Toneri|en|Prince Toneri|WD=Q1362200|lt=Prince Toneri}} with the assistance of {{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|WD=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro}} and presented to {{ill|Empress Genshō|en|Empress Genshō|WD=Q235343|lt=Empress Genshō}}.<ref>{{Citation | title = Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to AD 697 | author-link = William George Aston | first = William George | last = Aston | page = xv | chapter = Introduction | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | edition = Tra | date = July 2005 | orig-year = 1972 | isbn = 978-0-8048-3674-6}}, from the original Chinese and Japanese.</ref> The book is also a reflection of {{ill|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|en|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|WD=Q58381696|lt=Chinese influence}} on Japanese civilization.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref> In Japan, the Sinicized court wanted written history that could be compared with the annals of the Chinese.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref>
The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} begins with the [[Japanese creation myth]], explaining the origin of the world and the first seven generations of divine beings (starting with [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kuninotokotachi]]), and goes on with a number of myths as does the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, but continues its account through to events of the 8th century. It is believed to record accurately the latter reigns of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji}}, {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} focuses on the merits of the virtuous {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=rulers}} as well as the errors of the bad rulers. It describes episodes from [[Japanese mythology|mythological]] eras and {{ill|Diplomacy|en|Diplomacy|WD=Q1889|lt=diplomatic}} contacts with other countries. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was written in {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|WD=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese}}, as was common for official documents at that time. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}}, on the other hand, is written in a combination of Chinese and phonetic transcription of Japanese (primarily for names and songs). The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} also contains numerous {{ill|Transliteration|en|Transliteration|WD=Q134550|lt=Transliteration}} notes telling the reader how words were pronounced in Japanese. Collectively, the stories in this book and the {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}} are referred to as the Kiki stories.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.equinoxpub.com/books/showbook.asp?bkid=184 | title = Equinox Pub}}.</ref>
The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation|title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time|first=Christopher|last=Yorke|journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]]|volume=15|issue=1|date=February 2006|pages=73–85|url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|access-date=2009-08-29|archive-date=2006-05-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The first translation was completed by William George Aston in 1896 (English).<ref>Yasumaro no O.Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697.William George Aston.London.Transactions and proceedings of the Japan Society.2006</ref>

Background === The background of the compilation of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is that Emperor Tenmu ordered 12 people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the empire.<ref>''日本の歴史4 天平の時代'' p.39, {{ill|Shueisha|en|Shueisha|WD=Q844822|lt=Shueisha}}, Towao Sakehara</ref>
''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' notes that "{{lang|ja-Hani|先是一品舍人親王奉勅修日本紀。至是功成奏上。紀卅卷系圖一卷}}" in the part of May 720. It means "Up to that time, <!--一品-->Prince Toneri had been compiling ''Nihongi'' on the orders of the emperor; he completed it, submitting 30 volumes of history and one volume of genealogy".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Keizai Zasshisha |editor-link=:ja:経済雑誌社 |title=Shoku Nihongi |script-title=ja:続日本紀 |series=[[Rikkokushi|National History]] |language=ja |volume=2 |date=1897 |publication-place=Tokyo |publisher=Keizai Zasshisha |url={{NDLDC|991092|/1/187|format=url}} |page=362 |via=[[National Diet Library]] |doi=10.11501/991092 |id={{NDLPID|991092}} |author1=経済雑誌社 }}</ref>
===Sources=== The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is a synthesis of older documents, specifically on the records that had been continuously kept in the Yamato court since the sixth century. It also includes documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. Prior to {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, there were ''{{ill|Tennōki|en|Tennōki|WD=Q6141029|lt=Tennōki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kokki|en|Kokki|WD=Q826177|lt=Kokki}}'' compiled by {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}} and [[Soga no Umako]], but as they were stored in Soga's residence, they were burned at the time of the {{ill|Isshi incident|en|Isshi incident|WD=Q1062771|lt=Isshi incident}} in July 645.
The work's contributors refer to various sources which do not exist today. Among those sources, three [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] documents (''Kudara-ki'', etc.) are cited mainly for the purpose of recording diplomatic affairs.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7jDuhnI6r9UC&q=paekche+nihon&pg=PA40 Sakamoto, Tarō. (1991). ''The Six National Histories of Japan: Rikkokushi,'' John S. Brownlee, tr.] pp. 40–41; [https://books.google.com/books?id=x5mwgfPXK1kC&dq=paekche+nihon+shoki&pg=PA170 Inoue Mitsusada. (1999). "The Century of Reform" in ''The Cambridge History of Japan'', Delmer Brown, ed. Vol. I], p.170.</ref> Textual criticism shows that scholars fleeing the destruction of the Baekje to Yamato wrote these histories and the authors of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} heavily relied upon those sources.<ref>Sakamoto, pp. 40–41.</ref> This must be taken into account in relation to statements referring to old historic rivalries between the ancient {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea}}n kingdoms of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|WD=Q28456|lt=Silla}}, {{ill|Goguryeo|en|Goguryeo|WD=Q28370|lt=Goguryeo}}, and [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]].
Some other sources are cited anonymously as ''aru fumi'' ({{lang|ja-Hani|一書}}; "some document"), in order to keep alternative records for specific incidents.
==Exaggeration of reign lengths== Most scholars agree that the purported founding date of Japan (660 BCE) and the earliest emperors of Japan are mythical.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=wrc6rzKkbgcC&dq=Kigensetsu&pg=PA555 Rimmer, Thomas ''et al.'' (2005). ''The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature''], p. 555 n1.</ref>{{failed verification|sate=February 2015|date=February 2015}}<!-- The exact wording of Note 1 is "Empire Founding Day (Kigensetsu), February 11, was established in 1872 as the anniversary of the legendary Emperor Jinmu's accession to the throne in 660 B.C., which is said to have marked the beginning of the Japanese nation. After the Pacific War, it was abolished and then, in 1966, reinstated as Nation Founding Day (Kenkoku kinen no hi)." -- How anyone could read this as supporting the material in this sentence I don't know. --> This does not necessarily imply that the persons referred to did not exist, merely that there is insufficient material available for further verification and study.<ref name="kelly">Kelly, Charles F. [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/kofun.html "Kofun Culture,"] [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/index.htm Japanese Archaeology.] April 27, 2009.</ref> Dates in the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} before the late 7th century were likely recorded using the {{ill|Genka calendar|en|Genka calendar|WD=Q2513041|lt=Genka calendar}} system.<ref>Barnes, Gina Lee. (2007). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GLAo-bLJw4EC&dq=genka+reki&pg=PA226 ''State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite,'' p. 226 n.5].</ref>
For those monarchs, and also for the Emperors {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Ōjin}} and {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Nintoku}}, the lengths of reign are likely to have been exaggerated in order to make the origins of the imperial family sufficiently ancient to satisfy numerological expectations. It is widely believed that the [[:en:Epoch (reference date)|epoch]] of 660 BCE was chosen because it is a "xīn-yǒu" year in the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Sexagenary cycle}}, which according to [[:en:Taoist|Taoist]] beliefs was an appropriate year for a revolution to take place. As Taoist theory also groups together 21 sexagenary cycles into one unit of time, it is assumed that the compilers of {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} assigned the year 601 (a "xīn-yǒu" year in which Prince Shotoku's reformation took place) as a "modern revolution" year, and consequently recorded 660 BCE, 1260 years prior to that year, as the founding epoch.
===''Kesshi Hachidai''=== For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, only the years of birth and reign, year of naming as Crown Prince, names of consorts, and locations of tomb are recorded. They are called the ''Kesshi Hachidai'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|欠史八代}}, "eight generations lacking history") because no legends (or a few, as quoted in ''[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]''{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}) are associated with them. Some{{which|date=February 2015}} studies support the view that these emperors were invented to push Jimmu's reign further back to the year 660 BCE. {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} itself somewhat elevates the "tenth" {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin}}, recording that he was called the ''Hatsu-Kuni-Shirasu'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|御肇国}}: first nation-ruling) emperor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_oEfAAAAYAAJ |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |date=1896 |publisher=Society |isbn=978-0-524-05347-8 |language=en}}</ref>
== Influences == The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Yorke |first=Christopher |title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time |date=February 2006 |url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |access-date=2009-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2006-05-16}}</ref>

[[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Page from a copy of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (c. 9th century)]] {{Shintoism}} The {{nihongo|'''''Nihon Shoki'''''|日本書紀}} or {{Nihongo|'''''Nihongi'''''|日本紀}}, sometimes translated as '''''The Chronicles of Japan''''', is the second-oldest book of classical {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}. It is more elaborate and detailed than the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, the oldest, and has proven to be an important tool for historians and [[:en:Archaeologists|Archaeologists]] as it includes the most complete extant historical record of [[:en:Ancient Japan|Ancient Japan]]. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was finished in [[:en:720 in poetry|720]] under the editorial supervision of {{ill|Prince Toneri|en|Prince Toneri|WD=Q1362200|lt=Prince Toneri}} with the assistance of {{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|WD=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro}} and presented to {{ill|Empress Genshō|en|Empress Genshō|WD=Q235343|lt=Empress Genshō}}.<ref>{{Citation | title = Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to AD 697 | author-link = William George Aston | first = William George | last = Aston | page = xv | chapter = Introduction | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | edition = Tra | date = July 2005 | orig-year = 1972 | isbn = 978-0-8048-3674-6}}, from the original Chinese and Japanese.</ref> The book is also a reflection of {{ill|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|en|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|WD=Q58381696|lt=Chinese influence}} on Japanese civilization.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref> In Japan, the Sinicized court wanted written history that could be compared with the annals of the Chinese.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref>
The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} begins with the [[Japanese creation myth]], explaining the origin of the world and the first seven generations of divine beings (starting with [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kuninotokotachi]]), and goes on with a number of myths as does the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, but continues its account through to events of the 8th century. It is believed to record accurately the latter reigns of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji}}, {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} focuses on the merits of the virtuous {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=rulers}} as well as the errors of the bad rulers. It describes episodes from [[Japanese mythology|mythological]] eras and {{ill|Diplomacy|en|Diplomacy|WD=Q1889|lt=diplomatic}} contacts with other countries. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was written in {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|WD=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese}}, as was common for official documents at that time. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}}, on the other hand, is written in a combination of Chinese and phonetic transcription of Japanese (primarily for names and songs). The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} also contains numerous {{ill|Transliteration|en|Transliteration|WD=Q134550|lt=Transliteration}} notes telling the reader how words were pronounced in Japanese. Collectively, the stories in this book and the {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}} are referred to as the Kiki stories.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.equinoxpub.com/books/showbook.asp?bkid=184 | title = Equinox Pub}}.</ref>
The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation|title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time|first=Christopher|last=Yorke|journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]]|volume=15|issue=1|date=February 2006|pages=73–85|url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|access-date=2009-08-29|archive-date=2006-05-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The first translation was completed by William George Aston in 1896 (English).<ref>Yasumaro no O.Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697.William George Aston.London.Transactions and proceedings of the Japan Society.2006</ref>

Sumeramikoto, Shimo no maki.'' *'''Chapter 30''': ({{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}) ''Takamanohara Hirono Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' ==Process of compilation== === Background === The background of the compilation of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is that Emperor Tenmu ordered 12 people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the empire.<ref>''日本の歴史4 天平の時代'' p.39, {{ill|Shueisha|en|Shueisha|WD=Q844822|lt=Shueisha}}, Towao Sakehara</ref>
''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' notes that "{{lang|ja-Hani|先是一品舍人親王奉勅修日本紀。至是功成奏上。紀卅卷系圖一卷}}" in the part of May 720. It means "Up to that time, <!--一品-->Prince Toneri had been compiling ''Nihongi'' on the orders of the emperor; he completed it, submitting 30 volumes of history and one volume of genealogy".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Keizai Zasshisha |editor-link=:ja:経済雑誌社 |title=Shoku Nihongi |script-title=ja:続日本紀 |series=[[Rikkokushi|National History]] |language=ja |volume=2 |date=1897 |publication-place=Tokyo |publisher=Keizai Zasshisha |url={{NDLDC|991092|/1/187|format=url}} |page=362 |via=[[National Diet Library]] |doi=10.11501/991092 |id={{NDLPID|991092}} |author1=経済雑誌社 }}</ref>
===Sources=== The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is a synthesis of older documents, specifically on the records that had been continuously kept in the Yamato court since the sixth century. It also includes documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. Prior to {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, there were ''{{ill|Tennōki|en|Tennōki|WD=Q6141029|lt=Tennōki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kokki|en|Kokki|WD=Q826177|lt=Kokki}}'' compiled by {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}} and [[Soga no Umako]], but as they were stored in Soga's residence, they were burned at the time of the {{ill|Isshi incident|en|Isshi incident|WD=Q1062771|lt=Isshi incident}} in July 645.
The work's contributors refer to various sources which do not exist today. Among those sources, three [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] documents (''Kudara-ki'', etc.) are cited mainly for the purpose of recording diplomatic affairs.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7jDuhnI6r9UC&q=paekche+nihon&pg=PA40 Sakamoto, Tarō. (1991). ''The Six National Histories of Japan: Rikkokushi,'' John S. Brownlee, tr.] pp. 40–41; [https://books.google.com/books?id=x5mwgfPXK1kC&dq=paekche+nihon+shoki&pg=PA170 Inoue Mitsusada. (1999). "The Century of Reform" in ''The Cambridge History of Japan'', Delmer Brown, ed. Vol. I], p.170.</ref> Textual criticism shows that scholars fleeing the destruction of the Baekje to Yamato wrote these histories and the authors of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} heavily relied upon those sources.<ref>Sakamoto, pp. 40–41.</ref> This must be taken into account in relation to statements referring to old historic rivalries between the ancient {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea}}n kingdoms of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|WD=Q28456|lt=Silla}}, {{ill|Goguryeo|en|Goguryeo|WD=Q28370|lt=Goguryeo}}, and [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]].
Some other sources are cited anonymously as ''aru fumi'' ({{lang|ja-Hani|一書}}; "some document"), in order to keep alternative records for specific incidents.
==Exaggeration of reign lengths== Most scholars agree that the purported founding date of Japan (660 BCE) and the earliest emperors of Japan are mythical.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=wrc6rzKkbgcC&dq=Kigensetsu&pg=PA555 Rimmer, Thomas ''et al.'' (2005). ''The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature''], p. 555 n1.</ref>{{failed verification|sate=February 2015|date=February 2015}}<!-- The exact wording of Note 1 is "Empire Founding Day (Kigensetsu), February 11, was established in 1872 as the anniversary of the legendary Emperor Jinmu's accession to the throne in 660 B.C., which is said to have marked the beginning of the Japanese nation. After the Pacific War, it was abolished and then, in 1966, reinstated as Nation Founding Day (Kenkoku kinen no hi)." -- How anyone could read this as supporting the material in this sentence I don't know. --> This does not necessarily imply that the persons referred to did not exist, merely that there is insufficient material available for further verification and study.<ref name="kelly">Kelly, Charles F. [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/kofun.html "Kofun Culture,"] [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/index.htm Japanese Archaeology.] April 27, 2009.</ref> Dates in the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} before the late 7th century were likely recorded using the {{ill|Genka calendar|en|Genka calendar|WD=Q2513041|lt=Genka calendar}} system.<ref>Barnes, Gina Lee. (2007). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GLAo-bLJw4EC&dq=genka+reki&pg=PA226 ''State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite,'' p. 226 n.5].</ref>
For those monarchs, and also for the Emperors {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Ōjin}} and {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Nintoku}}, the lengths of reign are likely to have been exaggerated in order to make the origins of the imperial family sufficiently ancient to satisfy numerological expectations. It is widely believed that the [[:en:Epoch (reference date)|epoch]] of 660 BCE was chosen because it is a "xīn-yǒu" year in the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Sexagenary cycle}}, which according to [[:en:Taoist|Taoist]] beliefs was an appropriate year for a revolution to take place. As Taoist theory also groups together 21 sexagenary cycles into one unit of time, it is assumed that the compilers of {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} assigned the year 601 (a "xīn-yǒu" year in which Prince Shotoku's reformation took place) as a "modern revolution" year, and consequently recorded 660 BCE, 1260 years prior to that year, as the founding epoch.
===''Kesshi Hachidai''=== For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, only the years of birth and reign, year of naming as Crown Prince, names of consorts, and locations of tomb are recorded. They are called the ''Kesshi Hachidai'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|欠史八代}}, "eight generations lacking history") because no legends (or a few, as quoted in ''[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]''{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}) are associated with them. Some{{which|date=February 2015}} studies support the view that these emperors were invented to push Jimmu's reign further back to the year 660 BCE. {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} itself somewhat elevates the "tenth" {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin}}, recording that he was called the ''Hatsu-Kuni-Shirasu'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|御肇国}}: first nation-ruling) emperor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_oEfAAAAYAAJ |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |date=1896 |publisher=Society |isbn=978-0-524-05347-8 |language=en}}</ref>
== Influences == The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Yorke |first=Christopher |title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time |date=February 2006 |url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |access-date=2009-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2006-05-16}}</ref>

[[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Page from a copy of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (c. 9th century)]] {{Shintoism}} The {{nihongo|'''''Nihon Shoki'''''|日本書紀}} or {{Nihongo|'''''Nihongi'''''|日本紀}}, sometimes translated as '''''The Chronicles of Japan''''', is the second-oldest book of classical {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}. It is more elaborate and detailed than the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, the oldest, and has proven to be an important tool for historians and [[:en:Archaeologists|Archaeologists]] as it includes the most complete extant historical record of [[:en:Ancient Japan|Ancient Japan]]. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was finished in [[:en:720 in poetry|720]] under the editorial supervision of {{ill|Prince Toneri|en|Prince Toneri|WD=Q1362200|lt=Prince Toneri}} with the assistance of {{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|WD=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro}} and presented to {{ill|Empress Genshō|en|Empress Genshō|WD=Q235343|lt=Empress Genshō}}.<ref>{{Citation | title = Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to AD 697 | author-link = William George Aston | first = William George | last = Aston | page = xv | chapter = Introduction | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | edition = Tra | date = July 2005 | orig-year = 1972 | isbn = 978-0-8048-3674-6}}, from the original Chinese and Japanese.</ref> The book is also a reflection of {{ill|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|en|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|WD=Q58381696|lt=Chinese influence}} on Japanese civilization.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref> In Japan, the Sinicized court wanted written history that could be compared with the annals of the Chinese.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref>
The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} begins with the [[Japanese creation myth]], explaining the origin of the world and the first seven generations of divine beings (starting with [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kuninotokotachi]]), and goes on with a number of myths as does the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, but continues its account through to events of the 8th century. It is believed to record accurately the latter reigns of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji}}, {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} focuses on the merits of the virtuous {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=rulers}} as well as the errors of the bad rulers. It describes episodes from [[Japanese mythology|mythological]] eras and {{ill|Diplomacy|en|Diplomacy|WD=Q1889|lt=diplomatic}} contacts with other countries. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was written in {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|WD=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese}}, as was common for official documents at that time. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}}, on the other hand, is written in a combination of Chinese and phonetic transcription of Japanese (primarily for names and songs). The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} also contains numerous {{ill|Transliteration|en|Transliteration|WD=Q134550|lt=Transliteration}} notes telling the reader how words were pronounced in Japanese. Collectively, the stories in this book and the {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}} are referred to as the Kiki stories.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.equinoxpub.com/books/showbook.asp?bkid=184 | title = Equinox Pub}}.</ref>
The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation|title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time|first=Christopher|last=Yorke|journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]]|volume=15|issue=1|date=February 2006|pages=73–85|url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|access-date=2009-08-29|archive-date=2006-05-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The first translation was completed by William George Aston in 1896 (English).<ref>Yasumaro no O.Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697.William George Aston.London.Transactions and proceedings of the Japan Society.2006</ref>
==Chapters== [[File:Nihon Shoki 15 April 683.jpg|thumb|upright|The Nihon Shoki entry of 15 April 683 CE ([[:en:Emperor Temmu|Tenmu]] 12th year), when an edict was issued mandating the use of copper coins rather than silver coins, an early mention of {{ill|Japanese currency|en|Japanese currency|WD=Q6158487|lt=Japanese currency}}. Excerpt of the 11th century edition.]] *'''Chapter 01''': (First chapter of myths) ''Kami no Yo no Kami no maki.'' *'''Chapter 02''': (Second chapter of myths) ''Kami no Yo no Shimo no maki.'' *'''Chapter 03''': ({{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu}}) ''Kan'yamato Iwarebiko no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 04''': **({{ill|Emperor Suizei|en|Emperor Suizei|WD=Q313321|lt=Emperor Suizei}}) ''Kamu Nunakawamimi no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Annei|en|Emperor Annei|WD=Q313345|lt=Emperor Annei}}) ''Shikitsuhiko Tamatemi no Sumeramikoto.'' Sukitomo no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Kōan|en|Emperor Kōan|WD=Q312821|lt=Emperor Kōan}}) ''Yamato Tarashihiko Kuni Oshihito no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Kōrei|en|Emperor Kōrei|WD=Q313041|lt=Emperor Kōrei}}) ''Ōyamato Nekohiko Futoni no Sumeramikoto.'' **({{ill|Emperor Kōgen|en|Emperor Kōgen|WD=Q333572|lt=Emperor Kōgen}}) ''Ōyamato Nekohiko Kunikuru no Sumeramikoto.'' Nunakahara Oki no Mahito no Sumeramikoto, Kami no maki.'' *'''Chapter 29''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}}, second chapter) ''Ama no Nunakahara Oki no Mahito no Sumeramikoto, Shimo no maki.'' *'''Chapter 30''': ({{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}) ''Takamanohara Hirono Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' ==Process of compilation== === Background === The background of the compilation of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is that Emperor Tenmu ordered 12 people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the empire.<ref>''日本の歴史4 天平の時代'' p.39, {{ill|Shueisha|en|Shueisha|WD=Q844822|lt=Shueisha}}, Towao Sakehara</ref>
''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' notes that "{{lang|ja-Hani|先是一品舍人親王奉勅修日本紀。至是功成奏上。紀卅卷系圖一卷}}" in the part of May 720. It means "Up to that time, <!--一品-->Prince Toneri had been compiling ''Nihongi'' on the orders of the emperor; he completed it, submitting 30 volumes of history and one volume of genealogy".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Keizai Zasshisha |editor-link=:ja:経済雑誌社 |title=Shoku Nihongi |script-title=ja:続日本紀 |series=[[Rikkokushi|National History]] |language=ja |volume=2 |date=1897 |publication-place=Tokyo |publisher=Keizai Zasshisha |url={{NDLDC|991092|/1/187|format=url}} |page=362 |via=[[National Diet Library]] |doi=10.11501/991092 |id={{NDLPID|991092}} |author1=経済雑誌社 }}</ref>
===Sources=== The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is a synthesis of older documents, specifically on the records that had been continuously kept in the Yamato court since the sixth century. It also includes documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. Prior to {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, there were ''{{ill|Tennōki|en|Tennōki|WD=Q6141029|lt=Tennōki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kokki|en|Kokki|WD=Q826177|lt=Kokki}}'' compiled by {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}} and [[Soga no Umako]], but as they were stored in Soga's residence, they were burned at the time of the {{ill|Isshi incident|en|Isshi incident|WD=Q1062771|lt=Isshi incident}} in July 645.
The work's contributors refer to various sources which do not exist today. Among those sources, three [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] documents (''Kudara-ki'', etc.) are cited mainly for the purpose of recording diplomatic affairs.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7jDuhnI6r9UC&q=paekche+nihon&pg=PA40 Sakamoto, Tarō. (1991). ''The Six National Histories of Japan: Rikkokushi,'' John S. Brownlee, tr.] pp. 40–41; [https://books.google.com/books?id=x5mwgfPXK1kC&dq=paekche+nihon+shoki&pg=PA170 Inoue Mitsusada. (1999). "The Century of Reform" in ''The Cambridge History of Japan'', Delmer Brown, ed. Vol. I], p.170.</ref> Textual criticism shows that scholars fleeing the destruction of the Baekje to Yamato wrote these histories and the authors of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} heavily relied upon those sources.<ref>Sakamoto, pp. 40–41.</ref> This must be taken into account in relation to statements referring to old historic rivalries between the ancient {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea}}n kingdoms of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|WD=Q28456|lt=Silla}}, {{ill|Goguryeo|en|Goguryeo|WD=Q28370|lt=Goguryeo}}, and [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]].
Some other sources are cited anonymously as ''aru fumi'' ({{lang|ja-Hani|一書}}; "some document"), in order to keep alternative records for specific incidents.
==Exaggeration of reign lengths== Most scholars agree that the purported founding date of Japan (660 BCE) and the earliest emperors of Japan are mythical.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=wrc6rzKkbgcC&dq=Kigensetsu&pg=PA555 Rimmer, Thomas ''et al.'' (2005). ''The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature''], p. 555 n1.</ref>{{failed verification|sate=February 2015|date=February 2015}}<!-- The exact wording of Note 1 is "Empire Founding Day (Kigensetsu), February 11, was established in 1872 as the anniversary of the legendary Emperor Jinmu's accession to the throne in 660 B.C., which is said to have marked the beginning of the Japanese nation. After the Pacific War, it was abolished and then, in 1966, reinstated as Nation Founding Day (Kenkoku kinen no hi)." -- How anyone could read this as supporting the material in this sentence I don't know. --> This does not necessarily imply that the persons referred to did not exist, merely that there is insufficient material available for further verification and study.<ref name="kelly">Kelly, Charles F. [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/kofun.html "Kofun Culture,"] [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/index.htm Japanese Archaeology.] April 27, 2009.</ref> Dates in the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} before the late 7th century were likely recorded using the {{ill|Genka calendar|en|Genka calendar|WD=Q2513041|lt=Genka calendar}} system.<ref>Barnes, Gina Lee. (2007). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GLAo-bLJw4EC&dq=genka+reki&pg=PA226 ''State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite,'' p. 226 n.5].</ref>
For those monarchs, and also for the Emperors {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Ōjin}} and {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Nintoku}}, the lengths of reign are likely to have been exaggerated in order to make the origins of the imperial family sufficiently ancient to satisfy numerological expectations. It is widely believed that the [[:en:Epoch (reference date)|epoch]] of 660 BCE was chosen because it is a "xīn-yǒu" year in the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Sexagenary cycle}}, which according to [[:en:Taoist|Taoist]] beliefs was an appropriate year for a revolution to take place. As Taoist theory also groups together 21 sexagenary cycles into one unit of time, it is assumed that the compilers of {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} assigned the year 601 (a "xīn-yǒu" year in which Prince Shotoku's reformation took place) as a "modern revolution" year, and consequently recorded 660 BCE, 1260 years prior to that year, as the founding epoch.
===''Kesshi Hachidai''=== For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, only the years of birth and reign, year of naming as Crown Prince, names of consorts, and locations of tomb are recorded. They are called the ''Kesshi Hachidai'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|欠史八代}}, "eight generations lacking history") because no legends (or a few, as quoted in ''[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]''{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}) are associated with them. Some{{which|date=February 2015}} studies support the view that these emperors were invented to push Jimmu's reign further back to the year 660 BCE. {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} itself somewhat elevates the "tenth" {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin}}, recording that he was called the ''Hatsu-Kuni-Shirasu'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|御肇国}}: first nation-ruling) emperor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_oEfAAAAYAAJ |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |date=1896 |publisher=Society |isbn=978-0-524-05347-8 |language=en}}</ref>
== Influences == The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Yorke |first=Christopher |title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time |date=February 2006 |url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |access-date=2009-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2006-05-16}}</ref>

[[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Page from a copy of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (c. 9th century)]] {{Shintoism}} The {{nihongo|'''''Nihon Shoki'''''|日本書紀}} or {{Nihongo|'''''Nihongi'''''|日本紀}}, sometimes translated as '''''The Chronicles of Japan''''', is the second-oldest book of classical {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history}}. It is more elaborate and detailed than the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, the oldest, and has proven to be an important tool for historians and [[:en:Archaeologists|Archaeologists]] as it includes the most complete extant historical record of [[:en:Ancient Japan|Ancient Japan]]. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was finished in [[:en:720 in poetry|720]] under the editorial supervision of {{ill|Prince Toneri|en|Prince Toneri|WD=Q1362200|lt=Prince Toneri}} with the assistance of {{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|WD=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro}} and presented to {{ill|Empress Genshō|en|Empress Genshō|WD=Q235343|lt=Empress Genshō}}.<ref>{{Citation | title = Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to AD 697 | author-link = William George Aston | first = William George | last = Aston | page = xv | chapter = Introduction | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | edition = Tra | date = July 2005 | orig-year = 1972 | isbn = 978-0-8048-3674-6}}, from the original Chinese and Japanese.</ref> The book is also a reflection of {{ill|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|en|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|WD=Q58381696|lt=Chinese influence}} on Japanese civilization.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref> In Japan, the Sinicized court wanted written history that could be compared with the annals of the Chinese.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref>
The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} begins with the [[Japanese creation myth]], explaining the origin of the world and the first seven generations of divine beings (starting with [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kuninotokotachi]]), and goes on with a number of myths as does the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, but continues its account through to events of the 8th century. It is believed to record accurately the latter reigns of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji}}, {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō}}. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} focuses on the merits of the virtuous {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=rulers}} as well as the errors of the bad rulers. It describes episodes from [[Japanese mythology|mythological]] eras and {{ill|Diplomacy|en|Diplomacy|WD=Q1889|lt=diplomatic}} contacts with other countries. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was written in {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|WD=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese}}, as was common for official documents at that time. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}}, on the other hand, is written in a combination of Chinese and phonetic transcription of Japanese (primarily for names and songs). The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} also contains numerous {{ill|Transliteration|en|Transliteration|WD=Q134550|lt=Transliteration}} notes telling the reader how words were pronounced in Japanese. Collectively, the stories in this book and the {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}} are referred to as the Kiki stories.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.equinoxpub.com/books/showbook.asp?bkid=184 | title = Equinox Pub}}.</ref>
The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation|title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time|first=Christopher|last=Yorke|journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]]|volume=15|issue=1|date=February 2006|pages=73–85|url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|access-date=2009-08-29|archive-date=2006-05-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The first translation was completed by William George Aston in 1896 (English).<ref>Yasumaro no O.Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697.William George Aston.London.Transactions and proceedings of the Japan Society.2006</ref>

Background === The background of the compilation of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is that Emperor Tenmu ordered 12 people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the empire.<ref>''日本の歴史4 天平の時代'' p.39, {{ill|Shueisha|en|Shueisha|WD=Q844822|lt=Shueisha}}, Towao Sakehara</ref>
''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' notes that "{{lang|ja-Hani|先是一品舍人親王奉勅修日本紀。至是功成奏上。紀卅卷系圖一卷}}" in the part of May 720. It means "Up to that time, <!--一品-->Prince Toneri had been compiling ''Nihongi'' on the orders of the emperor; he completed it, submitting 30 volumes of history and one volume of genealogy".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Keizai Zasshisha |editor-link=:ja:経済雑誌社 |title=Shoku Nihongi |script-title=ja:続日本紀 |series=[[Rikkokushi|National History]] |language=ja |volume=2 |date=1897 |publication-place=Tokyo |publisher=Keizai Zasshisha |url={{NDLDC|991092|/1/187|format=url}} |page=362 |via=[[National Diet Library]] |doi=10.11501/991092 |id={{NDLPID|991092}} |author1=経済雑誌社 }}</ref>
===Sources=== The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is a synthesis of older documents, specifically on the records that had been continuously kept in the Yamato court since the sixth century. It also includes documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. Prior to {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, there were ''{{ill|Tennōki|en|Tennōki|WD=Q6141029|lt=Tennōki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kokki|en|Kokki|WD=Q826177|lt=Kokki}}'' compiled by {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}} and [[Soga no Umako]], but as they were stored in Soga's residence, they were burned at the time of the {{ill|Isshi incident|en|Isshi incident|WD=Q1062771|lt=Isshi incident}} in July 645.
The work's contributors refer to various sources which do not exist today. Among those sources, three [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] documents (''Kudara-ki'', etc.) are cited mainly for the purpose of recording diplomatic affairs.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7jDuhnI6r9UC&q=paekche+nihon&pg=PA40 Sakamoto, Tarō. (1991). ''The Six National Histories of Japan: Rikkokushi,'' John S. Brownlee, tr.] pp. 40–41; [https://books.google.com/books?id=x5mwgfPXK1kC&dq=paekche+nihon+shoki&pg=PA170 Inoue Mitsusada. (1999). "The Century of Reform" in ''The Cambridge History of Japan'', Delmer Brown, ed. Vol. I], p.170.</ref> Textual criticism shows that scholars fleeing the destruction of the Baekje to Yamato wrote these histories and the authors of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} heavily relied upon those sources.<ref>Sakamoto, pp. 40–41.</ref> This must be taken into account in relation to statements referring to old historic rivalries between the ancient {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea}}n kingdoms of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|WD=Q28456|lt=Silla}}, {{ill|Goguryeo|en|Goguryeo|WD=Q28370|lt=Goguryeo}}, and [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]].
Some other sources are cited anonymously as ''aru fumi'' ({{lang|ja-Hani|一書}}; "some document"), in order to keep alternative records for specific incidents.
==Exaggeration of reign lengths== Most scholars agree that the purported founding date of Japan (660 BCE) and the earliest emperors of Japan are mythical.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=wrc6rzKkbgcC&dq=Kigensetsu&pg=PA555 Rimmer, Thomas ''et al.'' (2005). ''The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature''], p. 555 n1.</ref>{{failed verification|sate=February 2015|date=February 2015}}<!-- The exact wording of Note 1 is "Empire Founding Day (Kigensetsu), February 11, was established in 1872 as the anniversary of the legendary Emperor Jinmu's accession to the throne in 660 B.C., which is said to have marked the beginning of the Japanese nation. After the Pacific War, it was abolished and then, in 1966, reinstated as Nation Founding Day (Kenkoku kinen no hi)." -- How anyone could read this as supporting the material in this sentence I don't know. --> This does not necessarily imply that the persons referred to did not exist, merely that there is insufficient material available for further verification and study.<ref name="kelly">Kelly, Charles F. [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/kofun.html "Kofun Culture,"] [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/index.htm Japanese Archaeology.] April 27, 2009.</ref> Dates in the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} before the late 7th century were likely recorded using the {{ill|Genka calendar|en|Genka calendar|WD=Q2513041|lt=Genka calendar}} system.<ref>Barnes, Gina Lee. (2007). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GLAo-bLJw4EC&dq=genka+reki&pg=PA226 ''State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite,'' p. 226 n.5].</ref>
For those monarchs, and also for the Emperors {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Ōjin}} and {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Nintoku}}, the lengths of reign are likely to have been exaggerated in order to make the origins of the imperial family sufficiently ancient to satisfy numerological expectations. It is widely believed that the [[:en:Epoch (reference date)|epoch]] of 660 BCE was chosen because it is a "xīn-yǒu" year in the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Sexagenary cycle}}, which according to [[:en:Taoist|Taoist]] beliefs was an appropriate year for a revolution to take place. As Taoist theory also groups together 21 sexagenary cycles into one unit of time, it is assumed that the compilers of {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} assigned the year 601 (a "xīn-yǒu" year in which Prince Shotoku's reformation took place) as a "modern revolution" year, and consequently recorded 660 BCE, 1260 years prior to that year, as the founding epoch.
===''Kesshi Hachidai''=== For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, only the years of birth and reign, year of naming as Crown Prince, names of consorts, and locations of tomb are recorded. They are called the ''Kesshi Hachidai'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|欠史八代}}, "eight generations lacking history") because no legends (or a few, as quoted in ''[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]''{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}) are associated with them. Some{{which|date=February 2015}} studies support the view that these emperors were invented to push Jimmu's reign further back to the year 660 BCE. {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} itself somewhat elevates the "tenth" {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin}}, recording that he was called the ''Hatsu-Kuni-Shirasu'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|御肇国}}: first nation-ruling) emperor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_oEfAAAAYAAJ |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |date=1896 |publisher=Society |isbn=978-0-524-05347-8 |language=en}}</ref>
== Influences == The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Yorke |first=Christopher |title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time |date=February 2006 |url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |access-date=2009-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2006-05-16}}</ref>

[[File:Nihonshoki tanaka version.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Page from a copy of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} (c. 9th century)]] {{Shintoism}} The {{nihongo|'''''Nihon Shoki'''''|日本書紀}} or {{Nihongo|'''''Nihongi'''''|日本紀}}, sometimes translated as '''''The Chronicles of Japan''''', is the second-oldest book of classical {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history|1=History of Japan}}. It is more elaborate and detailed than the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, the oldest, and has proven to be an important tool for historians and [[:en:Archaeologists|Archaeologists]] as it includes the most complete extant historical record of [[:en:Ancient Japan|Ancient Japan]]. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was finished in [[:en:720 in poetry|720]] under the editorial supervision of {{ill|Prince Toneri|en|Prince Toneri|WD=Q1362200|lt=Prince Toneri|1=Prince Toneri}} with the assistance of {{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|WD=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro|1=Ō no Yasumaro}} and presented to {{ill|Empress Genshō|en|Empress Genshō|WD=Q235343|lt=Empress Genshō|1=Empress Genshō}}.<ref>{{Citation | title = Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to AD 697 | author-link = William George Aston | first = William George | last = Aston | page = xv | chapter = Introduction | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | edition = Tra | date = July 2005 | orig-year = 1972 | isbn = 978-0-8048-3674-6}}, from the original Chinese and Japanese.</ref> The book is also a reflection of {{ill|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|en|Chinese influence on Japanese culture|WD=Q58381696|lt=Chinese influence|1=Chinese influence on Japanese culture}} on Japanese civilization.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref> In Japan, the Sinicized court wanted written history that could be compared with the annals of the Chinese.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nihon-shoki | title=Nihon shoki | Mythology, Creation & History | Britannica }}</ref>
The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} begins with the [[Japanese creation myth]], explaining the origin of the world and the first seven generations of divine beings (starting with [[Kuni-no-Tokotachi|Kuninotokotachi]]), and goes on with a number of myths as does the {{Lang|ja-latn|[[Kojiki]]}}, but continues its account through to events of the 8th century. It is believed to record accurately the latter reigns of {{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji|1=Emperor Tenji}}, {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu}} and {{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō|1=Empress Jitō}}. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} focuses on the merits of the virtuous {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=rulers|1=Emperor of Japan}} as well as the errors of the bad rulers. It describes episodes from [[Japanese mythology|mythological]] eras and {{ill|Diplomacy|en|Diplomacy|WD=Q1889|lt=diplomatic|1=Diplomacy}} contacts with other countries. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} was written in {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|WD=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese|1=Classical Chinese}}, as was common for official documents at that time. The {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}}, on the other hand, is written in a combination of Chinese and phonetic transcription of Japanese (primarily for names and songs). The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} also contains numerous {{ill|Transliteration|en|Transliteration|WD=Q134550|lt=Transliteration|1=Transliteration}} notes telling the reader how words were pronounced in Japanese. Collectively, the stories in this book and the {{Lang|ja-latn|Kojiki}} are referred to as the Kiki stories.<ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.equinoxpub.com/books/showbook.asp?bkid=184 | title = Equinox Pub}}.</ref>
The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi|1=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle|1=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel|1=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation|title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time|first=Christopher|last=Yorke|journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]]|volume=15|issue=1|date=February 2006|pages=73–85|url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|access-date=2009-08-29|archive-date=2006-05-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
The first translation was completed by William George Aston in 1896 (English).<ref>Yasumaro no O.Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697.William George Aston.London.Transactions and proceedings of the Japan Society.2006</ref>

Kōgyoku|en|Empress Kōgyoku|WD=Q235296|lt=Empress Kōgyoku|1=Empress Kōgyoku}}) ''Ame Toyotakara Ikashi Hitarashi no Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 25''': ([[Emperor Kōtoku]]) ''Ame Yorozu Toyohi no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 26''': ([[:en:Empress Saimei|Empress Saimei]]) ''Ame Toyotakara Ikashi Hitarashi no Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 27''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenji|en|Emperor Tenji|WD=Q314802|lt=Emperor Tenji|1=Emperor Tenji}}) ''Ame Mikoto Hirakasuwake no Sumeramikoto.'' *'''Chapter 28''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu}}, first chapter) ''Ama no Nunakahara Oki no Mahito no Sumeramikoto, Kami no maki.'' *'''Chapter 29''': ({{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu}}, second chapter) ''Ama no Nunakahara Oki no Mahito no Sumeramikoto, Shimo no maki.'' *'''Chapter 30''': ({{ill|Empress Jitō|en|Empress Jitō|WD=Q232026|lt=Empress Jitō|1=Empress Jitō}}) ''Takamanohara Hirono Hime no Sumeramikoto.'' ==Process of compilation== === Background === The background of the compilation of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is that Emperor Tenmu ordered 12 people, including Prince Kawashima, to edit the old history of the empire.<ref>''日本の歴史4 天平の時代'' p.39, {{ill|Shueisha|en|Shueisha|WD=Q844822|lt=Shueisha|1=Shueisha}}, Towao Sakehara</ref>
''[[Shoku Nihongi]]'' notes that "{{lang|ja-Hani|先是一品舍人親王奉勅修日本紀。至是功成奏上。紀卅卷系圖一卷}}" in the part of May 720. It means "Up to that time, <!--一品-->Prince Toneri had been compiling ''Nihongi'' on the orders of the emperor; he completed it, submitting 30 volumes of history and one volume of genealogy".<ref>{{cite book |editor=Keizai Zasshisha |editor-link=:ja:経済雑誌社 |title=Shoku Nihongi |script-title=ja:続日本紀 |series=[[Rikkokushi|National History]] |language=ja |volume=2 |date=1897 |publication-place=Tokyo |publisher=Keizai Zasshisha |url={{NDLDC|991092|/1/187|format=url}} |page=362 |via=[[National Diet Library]] |doi=10.11501/991092 |id={{NDLPID|991092}} |author1=経済雑誌社 }}</ref>
===Sources=== The {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} is a synthesis of older documents, specifically on the records that had been continuously kept in the Yamato court since the sixth century. It also includes documents and folklore submitted by clans serving the court. Prior to {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}, there were ''{{ill|Tennōki|en|Tennōki|WD=Q6141029|lt=Tennōki|1=Tennōki}}'' and ''{{ill|Kokki|en|Kokki|WD=Q826177|lt=Kokki|1=Kokki}}'' compiled by {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}} and [[Soga no Umako]], but as they were stored in Soga's residence, they were burned at the time of the {{ill|Isshi incident|en|Isshi incident|WD=Q1062771|lt=Isshi incident|1=Isshi incident}} in July 645.
The work's contributors refer to various sources which do not exist today. Among those sources, three [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] documents (''Kudara-ki'', etc.) are cited mainly for the purpose of recording diplomatic affairs.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7jDuhnI6r9UC&q=paekche+nihon&pg=PA40 Sakamoto, Tarō. (1991). ''The Six National Histories of Japan: Rikkokushi,'' John S. Brownlee, tr.] pp. 40–41; [https://books.google.com/books?id=x5mwgfPXK1kC&dq=paekche+nihon+shoki&pg=PA170 Inoue Mitsusada. (1999). "The Century of Reform" in ''The Cambridge History of Japan'', Delmer Brown, ed. Vol. I], p.170.</ref> Textual criticism shows that scholars fleeing the destruction of the Baekje to Yamato wrote these histories and the authors of the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} heavily relied upon those sources.<ref>Sakamoto, pp. 40–41.</ref> This must be taken into account in relation to statements referring to old historic rivalries between the ancient {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}}n kingdoms of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|WD=Q28456|lt=Silla|1=Silla}}, {{ill|Goguryeo|en|Goguryeo|WD=Q28370|lt=Goguryeo|1=Goguryeo}}, and [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]].
Some other sources are cited anonymously as ''aru fumi'' ({{lang|ja-Hani|一書}}; "some document"), in order to keep alternative records for specific incidents.
==Exaggeration of reign lengths== Most scholars agree that the purported founding date of Japan (660 BCE) and the earliest emperors of Japan are mythical.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=wrc6rzKkbgcC&dq=Kigensetsu&pg=PA555 Rimmer, Thomas ''et al.'' (2005). ''The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature''], p. 555 n1.</ref>{{failed verification|sate=February 2015|date=February 2015}}<!-- The exact wording of Note 1 is "Empire Founding Day (Kigensetsu), February 11, was established in 1872 as the anniversary of the legendary Emperor Jinmu's accession to the throne in 660 B.C., which is said to have marked the beginning of the Japanese nation. After the Pacific War, it was abolished and then, in 1966, reinstated as Nation Founding Day (Kenkoku kinen no hi)." -- How anyone could read this as supporting the material in this sentence I don't know. --> This does not necessarily imply that the persons referred to did not exist, merely that there is insufficient material available for further verification and study.<ref name="kelly">Kelly, Charles F. [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/kofun.html "Kofun Culture,"] [http://www.t-net.ne.jp/~keally/index.htm Japanese Archaeology.] April 27, 2009.</ref> Dates in the {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} before the late 7th century were likely recorded using the {{ill|Genka calendar|en|Genka calendar|WD=Q2513041|lt=Genka calendar|1=Genka calendar}} system.<ref>Barnes, Gina Lee. (2007). [https://books.google.com/books?id=GLAo-bLJw4EC&dq=genka+reki&pg=PA226 ''State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite,'' p. 226 n.5].</ref>
For those monarchs, and also for the Emperors {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Ōjin|1=Emperor Ōjin}} and {{ill|Emperor Nintoku|en|Emperor Nintoku|WD=Q313119|lt=Nintoku|1=Emperor Nintoku}}, the lengths of reign are likely to have been exaggerated in order to make the origins of the imperial family sufficiently ancient to satisfy numerological expectations. It is widely believed that the [[:en:Epoch (reference date)|epoch]] of 660 BCE was chosen because it is a "xīn-yǒu" year in the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=Sexagenary cycle|1=Sexagenary cycle}}, which according to [[:en:Taoist|Taoist]] beliefs was an appropriate year for a revolution to take place. As Taoist theory also groups together 21 sexagenary cycles into one unit of time, it is assumed that the compilers of {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} assigned the year 601 (a "xīn-yǒu" year in which Prince Shotoku's reformation took place) as a "modern revolution" year, and consequently recorded 660 BCE, 1260 years prior to that year, as the founding epoch.
===''Kesshi Hachidai''=== For the eight emperors of Chapter 4, only the years of birth and reign, year of naming as Crown Prince, names of consorts, and locations of tomb are recorded. They are called the ''Kesshi Hachidai'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|欠史八代}}, "eight generations lacking history") because no legends (or a few, as quoted in ''[[Nihon Ōdai Ichiran]]''{{citation needed|date=February 2014}}) are associated with them. Some{{which|date=February 2015}} studies support the view that these emperors were invented to push Jimmu's reign further back to the year 660 BCE. {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} itself somewhat elevates the "tenth" {{ill|Emperor Sujin|en|Emperor Sujin|WD=Q333530|lt=Emperor Sujin|1=Emperor Sujin}}, recording that he was called the ''Hatsu-Kuni-Shirasu'' ("{{lang|ja-Hani|御肇国}}: first nation-ruling) emperor.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_oEfAAAAYAAJ |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |date=1896 |publisher=Society |isbn=978-0-524-05347-8 |language=en}}</ref>
== Influences == The tale of [[Urashima Tarō]] is developed from the brief mention in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}} ({{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}} Year 22) that a certain child of Urashima visited Horaisan and saw wonders. The later tale has plainly incorporated elements from the famous anecdote of "Luck of the Sea and Luck of the Mountains" ({{ill|Hoderi|en|Hoderi|WD=Q2716491|lt=Hoderi|1=Hoderi}} and [[Hoori]]) found in {{Lang|ja-latn|Nihon Shoki}}. The later developed Urashima tale contains the {{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle|1=Rip Van Winkle}} motif, so some may consider it an early example of fictional {{ill|Time travel|en|Time travel|WD=Q182154|lt=Time travel|1=Time travel}}.<ref>{{citation |last=Yorke |first=Christopher |title=Malchronia: Cryonics and Bionics as Primitive Weapons in the War on Time |date=February 2006 |url=http://jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |journal=[[Journal of Evolution and Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |access-date=2009-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516005834/http://www.jetpress.org/volume15/yorke-rowe.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2006-05-16}}</ref>
